--- title: "The multiverse and its critics" subtitle: "The debate about specification curves" bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib] --- The multiverse, or specification curve, is the method taught in the course, and this part of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) examines it on the Housing and racial bias case study, at the point at which the course builds the specification curve of the claim. The origins of the idea, the purposes claimed for it and the arguments that are now being made against it are examined in turn. In the course you run a multiverse yourself, fixing a specification in a preregistration, fitting it and reading your result against the 64 specifications of the curve presented on the [Specification curve](../curve.qmd) page. The claim, taken from a field experiment in which the original authors emailed public housing authorities [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts". The method is under live debate in 2025–26, the objections raised against it are serious, and the module aims to enable you to take a position in that debate. Throughout the module the Housing case study serves as the worked example, and an unusual one, because every specification agrees on it while its replication in the SCORE replicability study nevertheless failed. ## 1. Origins {#sec-origins} The founding statement of the idea is a paper published in 2016 by Steegen, Tuerlinckx, Gelman and Vanpaemel [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse], which starts from the construction of the data before any model is fitted. The authors observe that the conversion of raw data into an analysable dataset involves choices – which cases to exclude, how to code a variable, where to cut a scale – and that several options are usually reasonable. Instead of privileging one dataset, they propose to build every dataset that a reasonable set of choices could have produced and to run the analysis on each, so that the reader learns how much the conclusion owes to decisions which nobody would defend as the only right ones. The idea is related to the 'garden of forking paths' described by @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience: a researcher who makes each choice once, on the fly, has walked one path through a branching garden, while the single p-value at the end keeps no record of the branches. The 2016 paper states its ambition plainly, that "it should become standard practice to go beyond a single data set analysis and to acknowledge the multiverse of statistical results", and concedes at once what the critics would later press, that "performing a multiverse analysis will often be difficult, and to a large extent subjective" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710]. The authors also sketched the extension put into practice by a curve of models, a *model* multiverse, in which "One specific analysis thus corresponds to a single sample from a model multiverse" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710]. The multiverse constructed in that paper was *customised for critique*, in the sense that the alternative datasets corresponded to choices which the authors of the target study "might themselves have considered", drawn from the earlier publications of the same team. It was therefore a post-mortem on the flexibility of one team rather than a general survey of the ways in which the question could be answered, a distinction which becomes relevant again in section 2. Steegen and colleagues also place the idea in an older lineage running through perturbation and sensitivity analysis in economics and Bayesian statistics, to which the 2016 paper added the demand that the whole distribution of results be shown. The modelling side was developed separately as **specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis], which enumerates the defensible ways of specifying a test, estimates all of them, plots the estimates in order and, in its full form, tests the curve as a whole against a null distribution built by permutation, that is, by reshuffling the data so that any true effect is removed. It is this display that the course adopts on its Specification curve page. A distinct strand of work kept the data and the question fixed and varied the *analysts*: 29 teams answering one question about football referees with odds ratios from 0.89 to 2.93 [@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne]; 73 teams testing one hypothesis about immigration and social policy, with more than 95% of the variance in their results left unexplained even after coding every identifiable decision in the workflow of every team [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]; and the SCORE robustness study, in which 457 reanalysts carried out 504 reanalyses of claims from 100 published studies [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The Housing case study is drawn from one of those hundred studies, and the five reanalysts who examined its claim are presented on the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-reanalysts). A further strand proposes Bayesian hierarchical models for aggregating data of this kind [@HoogeveenEtAl2020ImprovingStatisticalAnalysis]. The course combines these strands, treating the specification curve of the claim as a model multiverse, and the five analysts in the robustness study, together with the class chart, as a many-analysts layer placed beside the curve and meant to be read against it. ## 2. Three purposes {#sec-purposes} Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman pose the question that organises the current debate, namely what a multiverse is *for*. The three authors distinguish three uses, "as a tool for reflection and critique, as a persuasive tool, as a serious inferential tool", and attach a failure to each: "it fails as a persuasive tool when researchers disagree about which variations should be included in the analysis", and "it fails as a serious inferential tool when the included analyses do not target a coherent estimand" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1]. Their conclusion is mild, in that the multiverse "does remain a valuable tool", even though the authors "urge against taking it too seriously" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1]. The three purposes impose different rules for building a set of specifications. A multiverse built for critique may mix analyses that answer slightly different questions, since its aim is to show that researchers plausibly disagree about the question, and "it may be perfectly sensible to include analyses with different estimands as long as it is plausible that researchers may try out different estimands" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. Such a set cannot then be read as inference about one quantity, and Hullman formulates the condition in a companion blog post: "what kinds of equivalence are needed will also depend on your goal in using a multiverse" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood]. It is for that reason that the course builds its artefacts to different rules. The [specification menu](../menu.qmd) of eleven decisions, the [decision map](../menu.qmd#map) and the class chart serve reflection, since these three artefacts make visible how much a result depends on decisions that look arbitrary from outside, and they display options that answer other questions alongside the options that answer the claim. The curve of 64 specifications, by contrast, is built to the standard that inference would require and is used to persuade, every specification on it being meant to answer the claim as the course reads it, while the two decisions that leave two estimands on it, the comparison group and the emails counted, are named as such. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it Assign each artefact of the course to one of the three purposes: the specification menu, the preregistration of Task 5, the curve of 64, the randomisation test stored for each specification, and the class chart. For each, write one sentence on what the set of specifications would have to look like for that purpose to be served. Note where one set of analyses is being used for two purposes. ::: ## 3. The pruning critique {#sec-auspurg} The most direct empirical disagreement in the recent literature is the one between a study of model uncertainty by Ganslmeier and Vlandas and Katrin Auspurg's reply to it. Crossing five dimensions of specification at once, across four literatures of political science, Ganslmeier and Vlandas produce about 3.6 billion estimates. The two authors find that "the sign and statistical significance of estimates is more contingent on the underlying sample and the operationalization of indicators than on the inclusion of the control set" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6], and they state the dilemma themselves: "Running all possible models risks introducing errors in the empirical approach, but selecting a subset of robustness checks risks reintroducing the 'researcher's degree of freedom'" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 2]. Auspurg replies that "Multiverse analyses are only informative when all included models represent equally plausible strategies for estimating the same estimand" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. Her charge is that the set assembled by Ganslmeier and Vlandas is heterogeneous, both in statistical quality and in what each model estimates, with the result that its distribution pools numbers which cannot be compared. She names four kinds of nonequivalence: statistically inferior models ("Many models do not include fixed effects or cluster-robust SE, which are standard in panel data analyses" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]); unstable country subsets; causal misspecification from randomly combined covariates; and measurement nonequivalence, where "Outcomes differ in scope … and are sometimes negatively correlated. This clearly indicates that they do not reflect the same construct" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. When the set is restricted to the 1,152 models that she classes as justified, against 91,008 unjustified ones, a 60/40 split among the significant coefficients becomes one in which 97% point the same way. She rules out choosing models by their fit, noting that "Ironically, the authors' own fit criterion (AIC) consistently favors unjustified models" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1], and places the remedy before estimation, in "thorough, theory-based model selection" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 2]. The constructive version of the same demand is the rule of estimand consistency in Young and Cumberworth's book, under which "any 'necessary control' requires a clear causal diagram or definitional justification supported by prior research" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 57]. Young and Cumberworth are also explicit that "there is nothing in the distribution of estimates per se that tells us which is the true effect" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 119]. The course applied Auspurg's test to its own menu, asking, for every option of the eleven decisions, whether that option is a justifiable way of answering the claim as the course reads it. Of the 33 options, 18 are on the curve and 15 are not: 6 answer another question, 2 answer this one less well, 6 check an answer that the curve already holds, and 1 cannot be fitted on the public file. The options that answer another question, although they are off the curve, remain in the course, and @tbl-off shows why these options would not belong in a count of votes on the claim, in that each option gives its own answer to its own question. ::: {#tbl-off .cell tbl-cap='Options that answer another question than the claim, with the result that each gives on the Housing data: a difference in percentage points against the white names, as a difference in proportions with an HC2 test. Sources: `data/display_outcomes.csv`, `data/display_subgroups.csv`.'} ```{.r .cell-code} row_out <- \(o, cn, label) outcomes |> dplyr::filter(outcome == o, contrast == cn) |> dplyr::mutate(Option = label) row_sub <- \(start, label) subgroups |> dplyr::filter(startsWith(subgroup, start)) |> dplyr::mutate(Option = label) dplyr::bind_rows( row_out("reply", "hispanic", "Outcome: any reply"), row_out("reply24", "hispanic", "Outcome: reply within 24 hours"), row_out("named", "black", "Comparison: Black names, greeted by name"), row_sub("male", "Names: male names only"), row_sub("female", "Names: female names only"), row_sub("replies from officials", "Who replied: officials with Hispanic names") ) |> dplyr::transmute(Option, `Gap (points)` = fmt(b_pp), p = pe(p), Emails = n) |> tinytable::tt() |> tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Option Gap (points) p Emails
Outcome: any reply −4.8 p = 0.214 665
Outcome: reply within 24 hours 2.1 p = 0.642 364
Comparison: Black names, greeted by name −5.0 p = 0.328 371
Names: male names only −23.3 p = 0.0009 201
Names: female names only −15.7 p = 0.046 161
Who replied: officials with Hispanic names −25.7 p = 0.184 28
``` ::: ::: On the Housing case study the pruning arguably removes little that would change the picture of the claim itself. The options left off the curve give answers to their own questions, some of them in the direction of the claim on fewer emails or with less precision, and one, the speed of replies, in the opposite direction. Counted as votes on the claim, these options would mix questions, whereas retained as displays they describe the experiment. The decisions that remain on the curve change the size of the gap, but none of these decisions changes its sign. ## 4. One correct analysis {#sec-lakens} Lakens, Rasti and Tunç push the criticism further. Their target is the inference that many people draw from analytic variability, namely that, since reasonable analyses disagree, there is no single correct analysis and researchers should report distributions instead. The three authors separate random variation, which standard errors quantify, from uncertainty about which auxiliary assumptions are true – which measure is valid, which units belong in the sample, which adjustment set is right – and argue that the second is reduced by doing research rather than absorbed by wider intervals. Once the auxiliary assumptions are fixed, "there is a fact of the matter about which analysis correctly implements that test" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 7], robustness "is a consequence of valid tests, and not a goal in itself" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 15], and "Variability across specifications based on uninformed hunches, especially when less plausible alternatives are included, provides little actionable insight" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 10]. Their argument applies most sharply to the decision that dominates the specification curve of the Housing case study, namely which emails to count. As the claim concerns the tone of the replies that came, it points to the comparison among replies, yet that comparison measures a pure effect of the name only if the name did not change who replied, an assumption which the data cannot test. In the view of Lakens and colleagues, an analyst should settle which question is being asked, and argue for the assumption required by the chosen comparison, before the test, rather than report both comparisons and leave the reader to average the two. The assumptions on which each answer rests are examined in the [causal-graphs module](dags.qmd#sec-case). It is tempting to answer Lakens and colleagues with Task 5, in which you fix one specification before running it, but the two devices solve different problems. Preregistration solves a problem of timing, since it rules out choosing a specification after seeing where the numbers fall, a real worry, because "in the absence of preregistration, researchers may as well determine what is equivalent based on whether or not it supports their result" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 5]. The argument advanced by Lakens and colleagues, however, concerns warrant, which does not depend on timing, since an arbitrary choice remains arbitrary when it is preregistered. Of the two caveats that cut against the device used by the course itself, the first is that preregistering a reanalysis of data that already exist is a weaker form of preregistration, since "[w]hen the data already exist, authors can explore the data prior to registering their analysis" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 149]. The second is that the two approaches can be combined: "one could preregister a multiverse analysis to combine the strengths of both approaches" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9]. ## 5. The decomposition of the curve {#sec-forks} The variance of the 64 estimates can be split by decision, a split which on this curve is lopsided. Of that variance, 86.7% is attributable to the emails counted, 5.7% to the comparison group, 3.3% to the adjustment, 0.4% to the uncoded replies and 0.0% to the model, with 3.9% left to the interactions between decisions. Among the replies, the estimates range from −20.0 to −15.8 points, and among all delivered emails from −13.3 to −12.1. Figures like these invite the reading that the estimates spread along the curve all refer to a single quantity. The decision on which emails to count, however, is a fork of estimands. A gap among the replies and a gap among all delivered emails, with an email without a reply counting as no greeting, answer two related questions, which the curve names as two estimands instead of presenting the distance between the two gaps as uncertainty about one. Read in this way, the decomposition indicates where the argument has to take place, a use endorsed by every party to the debate. Lakens and colleagues "support the use of multimodel analyses to hypothesize about 'which analytical decisions are most consequential'" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 6], and Ganslmeier and Vlandas offer their method as something that "can help inform which combinations of choices are more or less warranted" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6]. On this curve, the decomposition indicates that one decision, which emails to count, needs a theory, while the choice of model or of covariates appears to matter little. ## 6. Frequency and probability {#sec-reading} One practical rule drawn from the literature that criticises the method concerns how to *read* a curve, and it prohibits treating frequency as probability. The share of specifications that support the claim, here 64 of 64 below zero with p < 0.05, describes a curated set of analyses and does not correspond to the probability that the claim is true. Rohrer and colleagues ask for variation to be "treated possibilistically", any result found anywhere in a justified set being a live possibility, and they attach a condition: "This possibilistic interpretation is only sensible if every universe included is indeed deemed justified" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. The Milliways project shows how standard displays emphasise how *often* an outcome occurs, thereby inviting "misleading, probabilistic conclusions" [@SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses]. Lakens and colleagues put it most bluntly: "Scientists should not compute the percentage of agreement across different data-analytic strategies, because we do not resolve scientific disagreement by majority vote" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 16]. Rohrer and colleagues add that a multiverse persuades only under a precondition: "This can only work if the results are fairly unambiguous across specifications" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 3]. The Housing curve meets this precondition completely, since every specification points the same way and clears the 5% threshold by a wide margin, and section 7 considers what such agreement settles about the claim. The live class chart on the [Class results](../class-results.qmd) page, on which every submitted specification appears as a mark over the curve, is best read as a many-analysts demonstration, the classroom analogue of the 29 and the 73 teams, with the extra property that every declared specification was fixed in a preregistration before it was run. Heyman and Vanpaemel, who run multiverse projects with students, describe the design as "comparable to the many-analysts-one-dataset approach used by Silberzahn et al. (2018)", and note that when several analysts each make their own choices "there is a multiverse of multiverse analyses" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 7]. On the Housing case study the class is likely to agree on the direction, the interest lying in the sizes and in whether the class, like the five analysts of the robustness study, reads the same evidence as support for the claim or not. Two of the analysts, 25N5D and P9W8Y, concluded in the first task of the robustness study that the data showed no evidence either way: one judged the claim by the size of its gap, which the analyst found significant but smaller than the twenty points stated in the abstract, and the other by a test that compared the female names alone (p = 0.13), before a significant gap in the second task. ## 7. Robustness and replicability {#sec-replicability} SCORE, the programme from which the robustness study came, subjected claims to three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. In that sense a multiverse, however large it is, remains a robustness check. Every one of its specifications is fitted to the same 1,014 emails, and a chance feature of that sample – a run of unusually cold replies to Santiago in one week of 2014 – would therefore be found by every specification together. The specifications, in other words, are not independent tests, and their agreement constitutes evidence about the analysis, given the data. The Housing case study separates the two properties cleanly. On the original data, all 64 specifications are negative and significant, ranging from −20.0 to −12.1 points, and the randomisation test stored for each specification yields at most p = 0.0030. The replication then emailed 3,050 housing authorities from new names, obtaining a logistic coefficient for the Hispanic names that was positive and far from significant (z = 0.66, p = 0.511). The curve could not have warned of this result, its specifications varying the analysis while holding the sample fixed, and the agreement among these specifications thus says nothing about how far a new sample might differ, which is what the confidence interval of any single specification describes. The candidates for the difference lie outside the curve: the names, which conveyed more than ethnicity; the authorities and the year; and the power of the original comparison, which leaves a significant estimate from a study of its size likely to overstate the effect, as the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-power) shows. Robustness to analytic choices and replicability are separate properties of a finding, and the Housing case study has the first without the second. ## 8. The multiverse in the classroom {#sec-teaching} Every side of the debate agrees that the multiverse is useful in teaching. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman concede that "the multiverse has been a valuable training tool" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 8], and Heyman and Vanpaemel build their teaching on it, with two rules that the course follows. The first places the reasons before the number of paths: "the goal should not be to merely devise as many paths as possible", and "[t]he key is that the alternatives are properly motivated" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 4]. This is why every option of the specification menu is presented together with its reason. The second is pastoral: "one should be cautious that students do not completely lose faith in (psychological) science" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9]. A day that follows a published claim through every defensible analysis, only to learn that a new experiment found nothing, could leave a class cynical. The case study can, however, also be read the other way, as an instance of research working as it should, with data that were public, a claim that five analysts and a class could check, and a replication that could test it. Hullman gives a further reason why this literacy is likely to matter more, namely that building a multiverse is becoming cheap, because "lots of forms of robustness checking that used to be difficult are now trivially easy" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood] once software can generate the specifications. When anyone can produce a curve on demand, the skill that arguably remains scarce lies in judging what belongs in the curve, naming the purpose that it serves, and refusing the readings that its construction cannot support. ## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources} The debate read here: @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources and the reply by @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; @RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood with the companion post by @Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood; and @LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne. The origins: @SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience and @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis, with a framework for judging which analytic decisions are equivalent in @DelGiudiceGangestad2021TravelersGuideMultiverse. The many-analysts strand: @SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne, @BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers and @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, and, for the diagnosis that many disagreements between analysts are disagreements about the estimand, @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial. The book-length guide is @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, the tools are @SarmaEtAl2023MultiverseMultiplexingAlternative and @SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses, and the classroom design is @HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom. Quotations from the PsyArXiv preprints are cited by the page numbers of the preprints. The numbers on this page are computed when the page is built, from `spec_curve.csv`, `menu_options.csv`, `display_outcomes.csv`, `display_subgroups.csv` and `analysts5.csv` in `data/`, which are described by their codebooks, and the replication of section 7 comes from the [background page](../background.qmd).
